title: Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
text:
In brief. When you try to work out what someone is thinking, which of their words should you pay attention to? I combined six studies, recorded over roughly 20 years, in which people watched recorded conversations and wrote down what they thought a speaker was thinking; the speakers had also written down what they were actually thinking. I transcribed 74 hours of video, labeled every utterance (question, suggestion, statement, and so on), and measured how closely each one matched the guesses and the real thoughts. Three results held up. Suggestions matched what speakers were thinking more closely, on average, than any other kind of utterance, questions included. The most recent words carried the most information. And it made no difference whether those words came from the speaker or from their conversation partner.

title: Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
text:
The question
Earlier research showed that people read each other more accurately when they can hear what is said. It had not asked which words, said when, and by whom. Research on conversation also treats questions as the best way to draw out what someone is thinking (Graesser & Person, 1994), so I expected questions to be the most revealing.

title: Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
text:
What I did
Turned video into text. An AI transcription model (Whisper) transcribed the video and research assistants corrected it. I hand-coded 5,000 utterances to train a model that splits speech into single utterances; on utterances it had never seen, it agreed with human coding 96.8% of the time.
Labeled every utterance. Four AI language models voted on whether each utterance was a question, suggestion, statement, agreement, and so on. The combined vote matched human coding 93.4% of the time, better than any published single model on this task.
Measured how close two sentences are. Every utterance, guess, and thought was converted into a sentence embedding so I could score how similar any two were in meaning.






In human words: how a computer compares two sentences



A sentence embedding turns a sentence into a long list of numbers that captures its meaning. “I’m nervous about the exam” and “this test is stressing me out” share almost no words, but their lists of numbers end up close together. Comparing two lists gives a similarity score, where higher means closer in meaning. That let me ask, for every single utterance, how close it came to what the speaker was actually thinking.


Modeled change over time. Bayesian models traced how similarity rose and fell over the course of each conversation, one study at a time, and then combined all six studies into a single estimate.






Note



74 hours of video, 1,346 observers, 956 speakers, and 11,906 written guesses. Transcripts are IRB-restricted and stay in the lab; this page shows model summaries only.

title: Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
Which Parts of a Conversation Reveal What Someone Is Thinking?
text:
What this is good for
The same pipeline would run on user interviews, support calls, or sales calls. For user research, the suggestions result is the practical one. Analysis usually focuses on how people answer the questions we ask them, yet the moments when someone volunteers a proposal (“it would be easier if…”) may say more about what they are thinking.

title: Zach Schroeder
text:
Email  GitHub  LinkedIn  Scholar  Résumé


How can we use language as a tool to understand empathy and interpersonal perception online and in person?
I’m a behavioral scientist and statistician with seven years of experience researching this question. Of my many research projects, some of my favorites include: building an analytic pipeline that transcribed and analyzed 20 years of video-recorded conversations to identify the best cues for understanding what someone is thinking; examining partisanship and outrage in ~8.6 million tweets discussing “cancel culture,” including how outrage builds and fades in the weeks after a cancellation; and a three survey experiments on how students’ gender and sense of belonging shape the way they read ambiguous feedback.
If I’m not wrangling data at my desk, I’m deep in the woods with my dog.

title: Belonging’s Role in Interpreting Ambiguous Feedback
text:
In brief. A professor tells a student, “This is a difficult major, many students do not persevere and instead drop out to study something easier.” Is that a warning or a vote of confidence? I ran three online studies (N = 1,125) in which students imagined hearing exactly that in office hours, then rated it, wrote about it, and used that feedback to pick next semester’s classes. Study 1 was exploratory, examining general trends in how students interpret academic feedback. Based on the findings from Study 1, Study 2 preregistered specific success criteria and replicated Study 1’s findings. Study 3 then extended the findings to test their robustness. Men read the comment more positively than women in all three studies; students who felt they belonged socially in their major read it more positively in two of the three. And students who read it more positively subsequently reported using the feedback to pursue harder, more rewarding classes.

N = 1,1253 studiespreregistered replicationpower analysisopen-text coding3 trained codersQualtricsR

title: Belonging’s Role in Interpreting Ambiguous Feedback
text:
The problem
Research recommends feedback that is specific and actionable. Much of what people actually hear, however, is a passing remark that requires the feedback recipient to fill in their own meaning. Earlier work had found that men and women read explicitly negative feedback differently; however, almost nobody has tested the murky middle of ambiguous feedback, where most real feedback occurs. The same question comes up whenever an organization speaks to people in a sentence that could go either way (e.g. a status that reads “under review,” an error message, a policy notice).

title: Belonging’s Role in Interpreting Ambiguous Feedback
text:
What I did
Study 1, exploratory (n = 423). Participants read the scenario and rated the comment on four items (how positive it was, how confident the professor seemed in them, how they felt afterward, and whether they would go back for more feedback). They then chose between a difficult-but-fulfilling class and two easy ones, and completed scales for social belonging (feeling part of the major’s community) and intellectual belonging (confidence in their own ability). I used a program of model comparison to identify the clearest relationships between variables, which became the hypotheses for Study 2.
Study 2, preregistered direct replication (n = 233). Same materials. Before collecting data I preregistered the hypotheses, a power analysis (at least 200 participants for .80 power), the exclusion rules, and what would count as success: each estimate had to land within one standard error of Study 1’s, and the model’s R² between .03 and .10. All exploratory findings from Study 1 (feedback interpretation differed by gender and social belonging) replicated in this model.






In human words: preregistration



Preregistration means writing down your predictions, your sample size, and what will count as success before collecting any data, then posting it publicly with a timestamp. It keeps a researcher from moving the goalposts after seeing the results. It is the same reason a product team should decide what counts as a win before an A/B test starts.


Study 3, preregistered extension (n = 469). Expanded on Studies 1 and 2. Participants reported the grade they believed would earn them the ambiguous feedback as well as their real standing in the major. They also wrote about the conversation in their own words. Three research assistants coded every paragraph for how the writer saw themselves, the professor, and the interaction (inter-rater α = .76 to .88), and a sentiment analysis scored the three-word answers for positive and negative emotionality.
All three studies ran in Qualtrics under IRB approval.

Each dot is one study’s estimate with its 95% interval. The gold band is the success range set from Study 1 and written into the preregistration before Studies 2 and 3 were run. A filled dot landed inside it; an open dot did not. Left: how much more positively men rated the comment than women, on a 1 to 5 scale. Right: the change in rating for each point of social belonging. Hover for the numbers.







In human words: reading this chart



Before running Studies 2 and 3, I wrote down how big each effect had to be to count as a successful repeat of Study 1; that is the gold band. Each dot is what a study actually found, and the line through it is the range of plausible values. For gender, all three dots landed in the band, so the finding held up every time. For social belonging, the third study came in below the band, so that finding is less certain.


Gender replicated cleanly. Men rated the comment more positively than women in every study, by about 0.4 points on a five-point scale (average ratings of 2.09 to 2.60 for women and 2.52 to 3.04 for men), and all three estimates landed inside the preregistered range. The gap held after controlling for academic standing and for major (STEM, psychology, or other), which rules out the simplest explanation, that men just believed they were doing better.
Belonging replicated with caveats. Social belonging predicted a more positive reading in Studies 1 and 2, and Study 2’s estimate landed inside its range. In Study 3 the effect pointed the same way but was too small to meet the criterion. Study 3 ran in fall 2020, for many participants a first term spent entirely online, which may have changed what belonging to a major even meant. Intellectual belonging never predicted how the comment was read, although men reported more of it.
The open-text answers told a more detailed version of the same story. In their paragraphs, men described themselves and the interaction more positively than women did, and in their three-word answers they used fewer negative words for how they felt. However, men and women did not describe the professor any differently.

Feedback perception predicted subsequent class choices. Students who read the comment more positively leaned toward the difficult-but-fulfilling class (controlling for gender), in Studies 1 and 3 (Study 2 pointed the same way but was not significant). In Study 3, part of the gender gap in class choice ran through how the feedback was interpreted (indirect effect b = 0.07, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.14).






In human words: what an “indirect effect” means



Women were less likely than men to say they would take the harder class. Part of the reason ran through the feedback itself: women read the comment more negatively, and students who read it more negatively were less drawn to the harder class. The indirect effect measures how much of the gender gap travels along that path. It is small, but it suggests a single ambiguous sentence can nudge a real decision.

title: Belonging’s Role in Interpreting Ambiguous Feedback
text:
What this is good for
When wording is ambiguous, readers supply the meaning, and different groups of readers supply it differently and predictably. These effects are compounded when feedback is read without vocal tone or other interpersonal cues. For anyone who writes the sentences people see in a portal, a letter, or an app, a message has to be tested on the people who will actually read it.

title: How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
text:
In brief. Everyone has an opinion about cancel culture; very few of those opinions come with data. I collected 8.6 million tweets about cancellations from five samples: the phrase “cancel culture” itself, the “___ is over” hashtag trend, and tweets about specific academics, celebrities, and private citizens who were canceled. I estimated each user’s political lean from the words in their profile bio, then scored every tweet for moral and emotional language. Two findings stand out. Liberal- and conservative-leaning users discussed the same events in different moral vocabularies. And outrage did not peak when a story broke; it built over the following week or two.

8.6M tweets4M users5 samplespartisan lean from biosmoral languagetopic modelingPythonRHPC

title: How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
text:
The question
“Cancel culture” gets invoked with a great deal of confidence and very little data. Underneath the argument are two questions any organization that listens to the public has to answer: who is talking, and how are different groups framing the same thing?

title: How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
text:
What I did
Estimated political lean from profile bios. A small share of users (1 to 9%) state their politics outright in their bio with terms like “#BlueWave” or “GOP.” I used them as anchors, then scored every other bio word by how closely it tracks those anchors across millions of bios. That produced an estimate of lean for a third to a half of all users.






In human words: reading politics from a bio



Picture a bio that reads “dog mom, nurse, #BlueWave.” The hashtag gives away her politics. The more interesting part is that “dog mom” and “nurse” now carry a little information too, because thousands of other bios pair those words with liberal or conservative signals. Add up those small signals across a whole bio and you get a rough estimate of lean for people who never mention politics. Rough is the important word: the estimate agrees only modestly with users’ stated politics (r = .28 to .43), so it is good for comparing large groups and not for labeling any one person.


Scored moral and emotional language. I measured moral language with a published dictionary of moral words and checked it against two AI models trained to recognize the same categories. The outrage score is the rate of words about harm, cheating, betrayal, subversion, and degradation. I also ran AI classifiers for anger, sentiment, and irony.
Found topics and tracked time. A topic model sorted 3.9 million tweets into 10 themes without any categories supplied by me. For 57 people with a datable cancellation, I lined up their tweets by the day attention peaked and followed the outrage score for a month on either side.






Note



8,572,185 English-language tweets from 4,035,488 users, collected in late 2022 through Twitter’s research API. Platform terms prohibit sharing tweet or bio text, so everything here is an aggregate. Code: github.com/zjschroeder/Cancel-Culture-Text-Analysis.

title: How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
text:
What I found
Liberal and conservative users brought different moral lenses to the same events. Each cell below compares how often conservative- and liberal-leaning users used one kind of moral language in one sample.

ml = FileAttachment("data/moral_by_lean.csv").csv({typed: true})
foundations = ["care", "harm", "fairness", "cheating", "loyalty", "betrayal", "authority", "subversion", "sanctity", "degradation", "outrage_proxy"]
foundLabel = new Map([["care", "Care"], ["harm", "Harm"], ["fairness", "Fairness"], ["cheating", "Cheating"], ["loyalty", "Loyalty"], ["betrayal", "Betrayal"], ["authority", "Authority"], ["subversion", "Subversion"], ["sanctity", "Sanctity"], ["degradation", "Degradation"], ["outrage_proxy", "Outrage proxy"]])
studies = ["Cancel Culture", "Is Over Party", "Academics", "Celebrities", "Civilians"]
ratio = studies.flatMap(s => {
  const con = ml.find(d => d.study === s && d.lean === "Conservative");
  const lib = ml.find(d => d.study === s && d.lean === "Liberal");
  return foundations.map(f => ({study: s, foundation: foundLabel.get(f), con: con[f], lib: lib[f], log2ratio: Math.log2(con[f] / lib[f])}));
})
Plot.plot({
  width: 720, height: 300, marginLeft: 110, marginBottom: 60,
  x: {label: null, domain: foundations.map(f => foundLabel.get(f)), tickRotate: -30},
  y: {label: null, domain: studies},
  color: {type: "diverging", scheme: "RdBu", reverse: true, domain: [-1, 1], legend: true, width: 360, label: "ratio, conservative / liberal (← liberal higher · conservative higher →)", ticks: [-0.7, 0, 0.7], tickFormat: d => d === 0 ? "equal" : d > 0 ? `${Math.pow(2, d).toFixed(1)}× con` : `${Math.pow(2, -d).toFixed(1)}× lib`},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(ratio, {x: "foundation", y: "study", fill: "log2ratio", inset: 1, tip: true, title: d => `${d.study}, ${d.foundation}\nconservative: ${(d.con * 100).toFixed(2)}% of tokens\nliberal: ${(d.lib * 100).toFixed(2)}% of tokens\nratio: ${Math.pow(2, d.log2ratio).toFixed(2)}`}),
    Plot.text(ratio, {x: "foundation", y: "study", text: d => Math.pow(2, d.log2ratio).toFixed(2), fill: d => Math.abs(d.log2ratio) > 0.6 ? "white" : "#111", fontSize: 11})
  ]
})












































Red means conservative-leaning users used that language more; blue means liberal-leaning users did. Hover for the underlying rates.







In human words: reading the heatmap



Each number is a ratio. A 2.00 means conservative-leaning users used that kind of language twice as often as liberal-leaning users; a 0.50 means half as often. So when the person being canceled was an academic, conservatives talked about fairness about twice as much as liberals did. When it was a celebrity, they talked about purity and sanctity about half as much. The colors are scaled so that twice as much and half as much look equally strong.


Fairness showed the biggest gap, but its direction depended on who was being canceled: conservatives used it far more when the target was an academic or a private citizen, and slightly less in the other samples. Betrayal, degradation, and outrage leaned conservative in nearly every sample.
They also talked about different parts of the story. Conservative-leaning users spent more of their tweets on free speech and on the idea of “the mob”; liberal-leaning users spent more on accountability and consequences. The gaps are a few percentage points, but they point the same way across millions of tweets.
Outrage built after the attention.

ev = FileAttachment("data/outrage_event_time.csv").csv({typed: true})
evTypes = ["Academics", "Celebrities", "Civilians"]
evBase = new Map(evTypes.map(t => {
  const pre = ev.filter(d => d.type === t && d.rel < 0);
  return [t, d3.sum(pre, d => d.outrage * d.n) / d3.sum(pre, d => d.n)];
}))
evRel = ev.map(d => ({...d, rel_outrage: d.outrage_7d / evBase.get(d.type)}))
viewof evShow = Inputs.checkbox(evTypes, {label: "Show", value: ["Academics", "Celebrities"]})
Plot.plot({
  width: 720, height: 340, marginLeft: 55, marginRight: 20,
  x: {label: "Days from the day of peak tweet volume →", domain: [-30, 30], ticks: [-30, -20, -10, 0, 10, 20, 30]},
  y: {label: "↑ Outrage rate relative to the month before", grid: true, domain: [0, 2.5], tickFormat: d => d + "×"},
  color: {domain: evTypes, range: ["#123F36", "#C49A45", "#8a8f98"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([1], {stroke: "#374151", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "#374151"}),
    Plot.line(evRel.filter(d => evShow.includes(d.type)), {x: "rel", y: "rel_outrage", stroke: "type", strokeWidth: 2.5, curve: "monotone-x", tip: true,
      title: d => `${d.type}, day ${d.rel > 0 ? "+" : ""}${d.rel}\n7-day outrage rate ${d.outrage_7d.toFixed(1)} per 1,000 words (${d.rel_outrage.toFixed(2)}× the month before)\n${d.n.toLocaleString()} tweets that day`})
  ]
})












































Day 0 is the day each person received the most tweets. Higher lines mean more outrage language than in the month before. Civilians are hidden by default because six cases are too few for a stable line.







In human words: lining up the timelines



Every cancellation happened on a different date, so I reset each person’s clock: day 0 is the day the most people were tweeting about them. Averaging those reset timelines shows the typical arc. For academics, the first burst of tweets carried little extra outrage; outrage roughly doubled about ten days later. For celebrities, it rose with the burst and faded within about ten days.


An anger score is not an outrage score. An off-the-shelf AI “anger” classifier and the moral-outrage measure were essentially unrelated, tweet by tweet (r = −.05). Which tool a team picks decides what it finds.

title: How Liberals and Conservatives Talk About Cancel Culture
text:
What this is good for
Interviews and surveys capture what people say when a researcher asks. A dataset like this captures what they say to each other. The same approach would work on support tickets, portal comments, or reviews: estimate who is talking, compare how each group frames the same event, and watch how the tone shifts in the days after something goes wrong.
